info.text: Sequencers usually measure fragments, not an intact chromosome from end to end. Reconstructing a useful genome therefore joins sample preparation and base calling to computational assembly, quality evidence, and biological annotation.

clusters.name: Preparing DNA fragments
clusters.fact: DNA is extracted, fragmented when needed, and joined to platform-specific adapters to create a sequencing library that an instrument can read.

DNA extraction.text: The isolation of DNA from cells or other biological material for downstream measurement.

fragmentation.text: Breaking DNA into a size distribution suitable for a sequencing method or library design.

adapter.text: A designed oligonucleotide joined to sample DNA so fragments can be amplified, identified, or read by a sequencing platform.

library preparation.text: Preparing DNA fragments, often with platform-specific adapters, so they can be sequenced.

clusters.name: Reading instrument signals
clusters.fact: A sequencing instrument detects signals from prepared molecules, base calling translates those signals into nucleotide letters, and quality scores retain uncertainty in each call.

sequencing instrument.text: A platform that measures physical or chemical signals associated with nucleotide sequence.

base calling.text: The computational conversion of instrument signals into proposed nucleotide bases.

base quality.text: A score expressing estimated confidence in a nucleotide call, commonly represented on a Phred scale.

clusters.name: Reconstructing longer sequence
clusters.fact: Assembly algorithms use overlaps and other linking evidence to form continuous contigs, order them into scaffolds, and estimate a consensus sequence despite repeats and gaps.

read overlap.text: A matching sequence shared by reads that can support their placement relative to one another.

contig.text: A continuous assembled sequence with no internal gaps in its consensus representation.

scaffold.text: An ordered and oriented set of contigs whose intervening sequence may remain unresolved.

consensus sequence.text: A sequence estimate formed by combining evidence from multiple aligned or overlapping observations.

clusters.name: Annotating biological features
clusters.fact: Annotation adds hypotheses and evidence about genes, repeats, and function to assembled coordinates; a genome browser presents those layers without making them identical to the sequence itself.

gene model.text: A representation of a gene's predicted or supported exon, transcript, and coding structure on an assembly.

repeat annotation.text: The identification and classification of repeated sequence elements in an assembled genome.

functional annotation.text: Associating genes or other features with evidence about products, roles, pathways, or homology.

genome browser.text: An interface for viewing sequence coordinates together with annotations and experimental evidence tracks.

bridges.fact: A sequencing read is the fragmentary sequence record passed from signal interpretation into alignment or assembly.

info.text: A nucleotide sequence inferred from one DNA fragment or molecule during a sequencing run.

bridges.fact: Coverage measures how much sequence evidence supports genomic positions; adequate depth helps distinguish a reproducible consensus from isolated measurement error.

info.text: The amount of sequencing data covering a nucleotide or genome, often summarized as average depth.

bridges.fact: Long-read technologies generate longer fragments that can span repeats and reduce ambiguity during assembly, though read length is only one dimension of data quality.

info.text: A sequencing read thousands to hundreds of thousands of nucleotides long, depending on the technology and experiment.

bridges.fact: The assembly provides the sequence and coordinate framework on which gene, repeat, and functional annotations are placed.

info.text: A representation of an organism's genome reconstructed from sequence data, at contig, scaffold, chromosome, or complete-genome level.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts are direct or near-direct instrument outputs, and which are computational reconstructions built from them?
lenses.explanation: Base calls and their quality scores form sequencing reads. Contigs, scaffolds, and the assembly are inferred by combining evidence across many reads.

reasons.base calling: It converts the instrument signal into proposed nucleotide identities.
reasons.base quality: It expresses confidence in an individual proposed base call.
reasons.sequencing read: It is the fragmentary sequence record produced by the sequencing workflow.
reasons.contig: It is a continuous consensus sequence reconstructed from overlapping evidence.
reasons.scaffold: It orders and orients contigs while allowing unresolved gaps.
reasons.genome assembly: It is the larger reconstruction assembled from sequence evidence.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts explain why repeated and longer observations can make reconstruction more reliable?
lenses.explanation: Overlaps and repeated coverage support a consensus, while long reads can span repeats that short fragments may not place uniquely.

reasons.long read: A longer fragment can bridge sequence contexts separated by a repeat.
reasons.read overlap: Shared sequence provides evidence that fragments belong together.
reasons.coverage: Repeated observations provide redundancy for consensus and confidence.
reasons.consensus sequence: It combines evidence across reads rather than trusting one measurement alone.
reasons.scaffold: Longer-range evidence helps order and orient contigs across unresolved sequence.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts turn reconstructed letters into hypotheses about biological structure or function?
lenses.explanation: An assembly supplies coordinates and sequence. Annotation predicts or records features and functions, while a genome browser lets evidence layers be inspected together.

reasons.gene model: It proposes the exon, transcript, and coding structure of a gene.
reasons.repeat annotation: It marks repeated sequence families and their locations.
reasons.functional annotation: It associates a genomic feature with evidence about biological role.
reasons.genome browser: It displays sequence, annotations, and evidence tracks in their genomic context.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts carry or summarize uncertainty as individual measurements become a genome interpretation?
lenses.explanation: Base quality describes individual calls, reads carry those calls, and coverage supplies repeated evidence. Consensus sequences and scaffolds summarize reconstruction, while a gene model adds a further evidence-based biological hypothesis.

reasons.base quality: It quantifies uncertainty in an individual nucleotide call.
reasons.sequencing read: It packages a series of measured base calls as one fragmentary observation.
reasons.coverage: It summarizes how much repeated read evidence supports genomic positions.
reasons.consensus sequence: It combines multiple observations into a sequence estimate.
reasons.scaffold: It represents longer-range order while retaining unresolved gaps.
reasons.gene model: It interprets assembled coordinates as a possible biological feature.

info.text: Place the sequencing workflow between molecular biology and the downstream interpretation of differences.

Use reads and reference sequences to reason about genomic differences.
